children: Futures tracking Canada's blue-chip stocks fell on Tuesday as rising bond yields globally and declines in precious metal prices dampened risk appetite, while an uptick in oil prices kept broader declines in check.
September futures on the S&P/TSX index (SXFcv1) were down 0.5% at 05:56 a.m. ET (0956 GMT).
Global bond yields hit major highs as renewed hostilities in the Middle East lifted oil prices, prompting markets to reassess expectations of interest rate hikes by central banks.
, a benchmark for prices across asset classes, rose to 4.788% — its highest since early 2025.
The yield on the Canadian 10-year note (CA10YT=RR) was at 3.739%, an over one-week high.
In a double whammy for resource-heavy Canadian markets, prices of gold and silver dropped 1.7% and 2.8%, respectively.
Elevated oil prices stemming from the Iran conflict are affecting the global economy, with many countries already raising interest rates to combat inflation.
U.S. Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh's Friday speech at Jackson Hole reiterated the central bank's stance on fighting inflation, raising odds of a hike this month.
The Bank of Canada is expected to announce its monetary policy decision on Wednesday, with markets largely expecting no change to rates.
Employment reports in the U.S. and at home later in the week could influence expectations of how the central banks will approach policy going ahead.
On the flip side, the 1.9% gain in oil prices kept overall declines in check.
The benchmark TSX marked its fifth month in positive territory on Monday, as miners posted a stellar rally in August on the back of rising metal prices.
Investors will also monitor developments in U.S.-Canada trade relations.
